topics: 🕯️ Doing Business With a Gentile Before Shabbat — kutach, ships, sieges, letters, rented utensils
🐕 Food Left for a Dog or a Gentile — no obligation to chase after it in the courtyard
🫒 Finishing on Its Own — Rabbi Yishmael vs. Rabbi Akiva on crushed garlic, grapes, and honeycombs after dark
🐐 Set Aside for Something Else — the muktzeh dispute of Rav and Shmuel
🍞 The New Mishna: How Much Roasting or Baking Must Be Done Before Shabbat

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Timing, Muktzeh, and What May Finish on Its Own
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 19a–19b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין צוֹלִין בָּשָׂר בָּצָל וּבֵיצָה אֶלָּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּצּוֹלוּ מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with a run of practical rulings about interacting with gentiles before Shabbat: how long before Pesach one may still sell kutach containing chametz, that food left for a dog or a gentile in a courtyard need not be chased if they carry it off, and how much lead time is required before renting utensils, sending letters, setting sail, or laying siege to a city. It returns to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's laundering custom and Beit Shammai's decrees, then takes up a new question: may one crush garlic, grapes, or honeycombs before Shabbat and let the liquid finish seeping out on Shabbat itself? That leads into the dispute between Rav and Shmuel over muktzeh — items set aside for a non-food purpose. The daf ends with a fresh mishna setting the standard for how much roasting or baking must already be done before Shabbat begins.

slides.title: 🕯️ Advance Notice Required Before Engaging a Gentile
slides.subtitle: A run of baraitot on how far ahead of Shabbat one must act
rows: Kutach is a spice used sparingly, so it lasts long enough to still be around on Passover
Renting utensils / sending letters to a gentile
Not on Shabbat eve; fine on Wed./Thurs.
Rabbi Yosei HaKohen was so careful that his handwriting was never found in a gentile's hand
3 days before Shabbat (unless for a mitzva)
Tyre to Sidon — a short hop — is permitted even on Shabbat eve
Laying siege to a gentile city
Once begun, the siege is not halted — even on Shabbat itself, per Shammai

callout.label: Food is different:
callout.text: One may put food before a dog or a gentile in a courtyard; if the dog or the gentile picks it up and carries it into the public domain, no one need attend to it, since the Shabbat prohibition never applied to either of them.

slides.title: 🫒 May Crushed Grapes and Honey Finish Seeping Out on Shabbat?
slides.subtitle: Two mishnayot, two tannaim, and a question about what 'kneading' liquid out really means

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Garlic, unripe grapes, and stalks of wheat crushed while it was still day — one may not finish extracting their liquid once it gets dark.

lines.speaker: R' Yishmael
lines.text: One may continue tending to them and finish after dark — the liquid comes out 'on its own' under the weight.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Is our mishna's rule — that whatever comes about on its own is fine — following Rabbi Yishmael?

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: No — it follows a different mishna: honeycombs crushed before Shabbat, whose honey seeps out on Shabbat, are permitted, per Rabbi Elazar.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But honey is food both before and after — no real 'squeezing.' Garlic and grapes go from food to liquid — that's true melacha!

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: A later baraita reveals Rabbi Elazar (with Rabbi Shimon) permits even olives and grapes — so the honeycomb case does extend that far after all.

callout.label: Resolution:
callout.text: Rava bar Chanina (citing Rabbi Yochanan) distinguishes: everyone agrees it's forbidden if the item was never ground at all; the dispute is only for items already ground but not yet fully pounded.

slides.title: 🐐 Why the Baraita Repeats Itself for the Gentile
slides.subtitle: One might think the dog's food and the gentile's food are governed differently

nodes.content: 📜 One may place food before a dog in the courtyard; if it carries the food out, no one need attend to it
❓ The baraita then repeats the identical rule for a gentile — why state it twice?
💡 One might have thought: the dog's food is the courtyard-owner's responsibility (he owns the dog), while the gentile's food is not his responsibility at all — so perhaps he may NOT give it to him
✅ The baraita teaches: even so, it is permitted — the same leniency applies to the gentile as to the dog

callout.label: Point of the repetition:
callout.text: Without the second clause, one might wrongly assume a stricter rule applies whenever the person eating the food is a stranger rather than the homeowner's own animal.

slides.title: 🐐 Muktzeh: Set Aside for a Different Purpose
slides.subtitle: Rav and Shmuel disagree across several parallel cases

boxes.title: Rav: Forbidden
items: Oil press mats/oil, ship-cargo mats — designated for a specific use, so muktzeh applies
A goat raised for milk, a ewe for wool, a hen for eggs, oxen for plowing, dates for commerce — may not be eaten or slaughtered
Follows the position that muktzeh is a real, meaningful category

boxes.title: Shmuel: Permitted
items: All the same items may be used freely, since Shmuel holds muktzeh mostly does not apply
A student who ruled leniently like Shmuel's view (following Rabbi Shimon) in Rav's own town was excommunicated — not because he was wrong, but for public disrespect
Follows Rabbi Shimon's position in the parallel tannaitic dispute with Rabbi Yehuda

callout.label: Not just theory:
callout.text: The Gemara also reports a dispute between two students about the best way to rescue possessions from a fire on Shabbat — one vessel at a time, repeatedly, or several vessels at once — paralleling a dispute between Rabba bar Zavda and Rav Huna.

slides.title: 🍞 New Mishna: How Much Must Be Cooked Before Shabbat?
slides.subtitle: Roasting, baking, and two Temple exceptions to the rule

steps.content: 1️⃣ Meat, an onion, or an egg may only be put up to roast if there is enough time for them to roast while it is still day
2️⃣ Dough or a cake may only be placed in the oven if there is enough time for its surface to form a crust before dark
3️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer is more lenient: enough time for just the bottom crust to harden
4️⃣ EXCEPTION: the Paschal lamb may be lowered into the oven right at nightfall, and the fire of the Temple's Chamber of the Hearth may be kindled right at nightfall too

callout.label: Why the exceptions work:
callout.text: Both exceptions rely on the same idea: the people involved — the members of a Paschal group, the priests tending the hearth — are meticulous about mitzvot and will not come to stoke the coals on Shabbat itself.

summary.principle: Whether dealing with a gentile, a fire, or food left to finish cooking, the recurring test is timing: enough must be done — or entrusted, or set in motion — before Shabbat that no further prohibited action need occur once Shabbat arrives.

flowSteps.content: 🕯️ Gentile dealings (ships, sieges, letters, rentals) each need their own measured lead time before Shabbat
🫒 Debate: may crushed garlic, grapes, or honey finish seeping out after dark? R' Yishmael permits, R' Akiva forbids

columns.content: 🐐 Muktzeh: Rav forbids using items set aside for another purpose; Shmuel permits
🍞 New mishna: roasting/baking must be substantially done before dark

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the Paschal lamb and the Temple hearth are exceptions precisely because the people tending them are trusted not to stoke the coals on Shabbat

quiz.q: Why is it permitted to leave food before a dog or a gentile in a courtyard, even if they carry it into the public domain?
o: Because carrying food is never forbidden on Shabbat
Because the Shabbat prohibition against carrying does not apply to a dog or a gentile
Because the courtyard owner is exempt from responsibility for animals
Because the food was placed there before Shabbat began
quiz.e: The baraita teaches that since neither the dog nor the gentile is obligated in the Shabbat prohibitions, one is not required to attend to or stop them from carrying the food out.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yishmael, what may one do with garlic, unripe grapes, or wheat stalks crushed while it was still day on Friday?
o: Nothing further may be done with them at all
One may continue tending to them and finish extracting their liquid after dark
They must be discarded before Shabbat
One may only finish them if a gentile does the work
quiz.e: Rabbi Yishmael holds that since the additional liquid comes out 'on its own' from under the weight, one may keep tending to the process even after nightfall; Rabbi Akiva disagrees.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Rav's and Shmuel's positions on muktzeh in the case of a goat raised for its milk?
o: Rav permits slaughtering it for food on Shabbat, Shmuel forbids it
Rav forbids slaughtering it for food since it was designated for another purpose, Shmuel permits it
Both forbid slaughtering any animal on Shabbat
The dispute only concerns oil, not animals
quiz.e: Rav holds that an item designated for a non-food purpose (like a milk-goat) is muktzeh and may not be used for food on Shabbat; Shmuel holds muktzeh largely does not apply, so it is permitted.

quiz.q: Why was a student who ruled leniently on muktzeh, in accordance with Shmuel's view, excommunicated by Rav Hamnuna?
o: Because his ruling was halakhically incorrect
Because he publicly ruled contrary to the practice of the local authority, Rav, in Rav's own town
Because he ruled on Shabbat itself, which is forbidden
Because he never studied the relevant sources
quiz.e: The Gemara affirms the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon (like Shmuel's leniency), but the student was punished for showing public disrespect by ruling against the accepted local practice in Rav's own territory.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, why may the Paschal lamb be lowered into the oven right at nightfall, unlike ordinary meat?
o: Because the Paschal lamb cooks especially fast
Because the members of the Paschal group are meticulous about mitzvot and won't come to stoke the coals
Because the Temple has no restrictions on Shabbat
Because the Paschal lamb is eaten raw
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the exception is due to the vigilance of the group members (bnei chavura zerizin hein), who can be trusted not to violate Shabbat by stoking the coals to speed the roasting.
